For liver malaria, it causes the person's complexion to turn dark, and they sigh deeply; their condition is like that of a dying person. Puncture the <term>Foot Jueyin</term> and draw blood.
For spleen malaria, it causes the person to have rapid chills and abdominal pain; when heat arrives, the intestines rumble. When the rumbling stops, sweat emerges. Puncture the <term>Foot Taiyin</term>.

These reach to the extreme. The *Royal Regulations* says: "To act falsely and firmly, to speak falsely and eloquently"—these are spreading rumors. If one fills this category, then the licentious words and novels of later ages that corrupt the heart and ruin customs, as well as false rumors that confuse the public, establishing sects, and gathering followers to preach—all these are of this kind. The *Royal Regulations* says: "Inciting the people" <gloss>altering the names of officials and things</gloss>, "making changes" <gloss>altering laws and regulations</gloss>, "holding to heterodox paths" <gloss>such as shamanistic witchcraft or popular prohibitions</gloss> "to disturb the government"—all these are inciting the people. If one fills this category, then the Buddhist claims of an "Empty King," the Daoists falsely establishing titles, the private creation of hermitages and monasteries, the use of talismans to control ghosts or heal illnesses, and the charlatans recklessly discussing fortune and misfortune—all these are of this kind. These two types of people, when residing within the village and party, incite the masses in their views and hearing. In terms of the Classics, those who do not follow the teachings of the Six Conducts can all be called these.

By multiplying the length and width, this equals 2,700 plots. Leaving one row empty for every one planted, and planting in one plot while skipping the next, one can plant 675 plots after excluding the empty spaces. Each plot should be 1 foot deep. Spring, Autumn, Winter, and Summer end to form a year. The <term>Spring and Autumn Annals</term> record human affairs, finishing the year by investigating and completing the details. The spring's warmth and autumn's coolness represent the harmony of the many political affairs, which is why it was chosen as the name. The <term>Guoyu</term> <gloss>Discourses of the States</gloss> records the gains and losses in the speeches and deliberations between the lords and ministers of various states. It is also called the "Outer Commentary" to the <term>Spring and Autumn Annals</term>, with Lu being the "inner" and the various states being the "outer," representing matters transmitted by foreign states. The <term>Erya</term> means "near"; it is the standard for closeness. <term>Ya</term> means "meaning"; it is the standard for correctness. The languages of the five directions differ, but they all take the "near and correct" as their main focus. The <term>Analects</term> records the words spoken between Confucius and his various disciples.

Lü Dalin says: "A humane person is one who treats the whole world as one body. The pain, itching, and suffering of others trigger my own heart of misery and apprehension. Thus, the whole world's suffering is the same as my own love. When there is a year of famine and the crops do not ripen, and the people have the color of hunger, the ruler, high officials, and scholars all share in the sorrow. It is not that the ruler cannot afford to eat, or that the officials lack fields and salaries; it is that the heart of a humane person shares with the people. # Chapter 74: Method for Making Fermented Fish

Generally, when making fermented fish <term>zha</term> <note>fish preserved by layering it with salt and cooked rice to trigger lactic acid fermentation</note>, spring and autumn are the ideal seasons. Winter and summer are not suitable. <gloss>In cold weather, the fish is slow to mature; in the heat, the process will fail unless an excessive amount of salt is used. However, if it is too salty, the fish becomes flavorless, and it is also prone to breeding maggots. Therefore, it is best to make [lacuna] fermented fish during these times.</gloss>

Use fresh carp. <gloss>The larger the fish, the better. Fatty fish are actually superior for this method; while lean fish are delicious, they do not keep for a long time. Select fish with a body length of at least one and a half feet, whose skin and bones are tough and hard, making them unsuitable for raw slices <term>kuai: thinly sliced raw fish</term>.</gloss>

These large fish are all suitable for making fermented fish <gloss>referring specifically to *zha*</gloss>. Once the scales have been removed, cut the flesh into slices. Each slice should be approximately two inches long, three inches wide, and half an inch thick. Ensure that every

slice has a piece of skin attached. <gloss>If the slices are too large or long on the outside, the exterior will become over-matured and damaged by the acidity before the center is ready, rendering it inedible. By the time the middle can be eaten, the meat near the bone remains raw and has a fishy smell that is unbearable to eat. Usually, one only takes the best third of the fish's meat for this. If the slices are kept small, they will mature evenly. The measurements provided are general estimates and do not need to be followed exactly. One should squarely chop the thick sections of the spine and take the skin and meat in thin strips. In thinner sections of the fish, take smaller but thicker pieces of meat. A slight shift in pronunciation resulted in <term>qingke</term> <gloss>highland barley</gloss> becoming noted primarily for its green color. The *Tang Shu* <note>original: "Book of Tang"</note> states that the Tibetan Empire <note>original: "Tubo"</note> produced <term>qingke</term>, yet the *Qimin Yaoshu* already used the name <term>qingke</term>, and its use is the same as <term>kuangmai</term>. It is likely that foreign dialects lack standard characters. For instance, the way people in Shanxi call naked oats <term>you</term> is based on the Mongolian language. The compilers of the *Tang Shu* translated a Chinese product as <term>qingke</term>; it did not necessarily originate from abroad. The *Tiangong Kaiwu* <note>original: "The Exploitation of the Works of Nature"</note> claims that <term>kuangmai</term> is produced only in Shaanxi and is called <term>qingke</term>, asserting it is barley that changes due to the soil, turning the skin dark green. This is merely a muddled guess and not based on actual observation.

<summary>The author clarifies that highland barley is a native grain, arguing against historical and contemporary misconceptions that attribute its origin to foreign lands or soil-induced mutations.</summary>
<keywords>Qingke, Etymology, Botanical Observation, Tiangong Kaiwu, Shaanxi</keywords>

### Method for Preparing the Supreme Treasure of the First Menses

Take the authentic first menses collected at the 5,480-day mark, whether from a vessel or silk. Wash it down with one bowl of freshly collected boy’s urine <note>original: "tong bian"</note>. Mix this with ten bowls of clear water and add one <term>qian</term> <gloss>approximately 3.7 grams</gloss> of alum. Stir it over a hundred times, let it settle, and pour off the clear water. Replace it with ten bowls of fresh clear water, stir and settle again, then pour off the water. 

Once clean, add one small cup of breast milk from a woman who has just birthed her first-born daughter. Place the mixture into a gold vessel and seal it with three or four layers of paper. Place it in the sun to dry for three days. Alternatively, seal the mouth with mud and place it in an ash-pot over a low "top-heat" <note>small charcoal fire</note> to simmer for three days. Remove it and grind it into a fine powder.

...Spirit will not intersect. Because of this, the stars and constellations fall into disorder, the sun and moon deviate from their paths, the four seasons are not harmonized, and the myriad things are not produced. This is truly because the operation of the fire in summer and autumn lost its rhythm, causing the conditions inside the cauldron to be inconsistently wet or dry.

"Wenchang records and oversees": the six stars shaped like a basket at the head of the Dipper are called the Wenchang Palace. The first star is the Great General; the second is the Secondary General; the third is the Noble Minister; the fourth is the Director of Fate; the fifth is the Director of Wealth; and the sixth is the Director of Calamities. The "Platform Assistants" refer to the four stars below the head of the Dipper. They are arranged in pairs and called the Three Platforms. They oversee all under Heaven, assisting the Empress from above. They regulate <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term>, follow the four seasons, and ensure the suitability of the myriad things below. They enable the high officials to each fulfill their duties. This serves as an image for how the cauldron receives the breath of Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things to bring about birth, completion, and transformation. If <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term> are already in conflict and the four seasons have lost their regularity, it is like a practitioner operating the fire tallies who makes excessive errors in adjustment. Therefore, the text speaks of "reproach."

When they lived in groups, there was no standard for bowing, rising, sitting, or standing. The sages, because of these natural divisions, created the Rites of respect and humbleness, nobility and baseness, elder and younger. They stored these within the context of palaces, clothing, food, and the acts of bowing, rising, sitting, and standing, in order to rectify ruler and subject, to distinguish superior and inferior, to differentiate father and son, and to order elder and younger brothers.

Thus, the great relations of humanity first became clearly manifest and could not be confused. Therefore, it is said: "Ruler and subject, superior and inferior, father and son, and elder and younger brothers cannot be stable without the Rites."

Serving as an official or studying under a teacher cannot be intimate without the Rites. Arranging the court, governing the army, positioning officials, and executing laws cannot be dignified or strict without the Rites. Praying, offering sacrifices, and providing for the spirits can be sincere and solemn even without the Rites.

...then you will achieve the proper state. There are also **wild silkworm cocoons** <note>original: 野蠶繭 (yě cán jiǎn)</note>, which are produced by wild silkworms living on mulberry trees. These are collected in every village, yet only the people of **Shuanglin Town** <note>original: 䨇林鎮 (Shuānglín zhèn)</note> use them for **reeling silk** <term>繅絲</term> <note>the process of unwinding the silk filaments from the cocoon onto a reel</note>. 

The method is as follows: Take the cocoons and dry them in the sun. Store them in a large bowl and soak them thoroughly with boiling water. Fish out the thread ends and place one cluster of cocoons into the cauldron, reeling them according to the standard method. When you reach the midpoint of the reeling, take another cluster to continue the thread. The water in the cauldron does not need to be heated over a fire; it only needs to be kept slightly warm.

### Making Silk Floss

Silk floss and reeled silk are equally essential for clothing and use. Any cocoons that are unsuitable for reeling into silk should be set aside. Once the reeling of the better cocoons is finished, these remainders should be used to **make silk floss** <term>制綿</term> <note>unspun silk used as padding for winter garments or for spinning into coarser thread</note>. 

The floss made from the first batch of silkworms is tough and durable, while the floss from the second batch is loose and soft. There are also those who produce it by using cocoon waste silk. In ancient times, it was said that only those fifty years of age began to wear silk garments, but today the people of **Huzhou** <note>original: 湖人 (Húrén); referring to the residents of Huzhou, a world-renowned center for silk production</note>—regardless of whether they are old or young—rely on this material to ward off the cold. Its qualities of being light, warm, and comfortable against the body are far superior to those of **cotton** <note>original: 木棉 (mùmián); literally "wood-cotton," referring to the cotton plant or tree cotton, which was a cheaper but less insulating alternative to silk</note>.

The rule states: place the denominators for **mutual multiplication** <term>hucheng</term> <note>original: 互乘 (*hucheng*); a technique for finding a common base when dealing with multiple ratios or fractions.</note> <gloss>7 men, 6 men; 48, 92</gloss>.
<note>A circular diagram features the character "Mutual" (互) at its center. Positioned above the circle are 7 men and 6 men. Positioned below the circle are 48 and 92.</note>
Multiply 92 chi by 7 men to obtain 644 chi. Also, multiply 48 chi by 6 men to obtain 288 chi. Summing these yields 932 chi, which is set as the **divisor** <term>fa</term> <note>original: 法 (*fa*); the number by which the dividend is divided.</note>.
As for the method: set the total cloth at 125,820 **chi** <note>original: 尺; a unit of length, roughly 32 cm during the Ming dynasty.</note>. Then, multiply the counts of men (6 men and 7 men) together to obtain 42. Multiplying the cloth by this yields 5,284,440 as the **dividend** <term>shi</term> <note>original: 實 (*shi*); the number to be divided in traditional Chinese mathematics.</note>. Divide this by the divisor to obtain a **military factor** <term>junshu</term> <note>original: 軍數 (*junshu*); a calculated constant used to determine individual shares.</note> of 5,670 for each. Multiply this by 48 and then divide by 7 <note>original: 七歸 (*qi gui*); "7-return," a method of division performed on the abacus.</note> to obtain trousers cloth. Also, multiply the military factor by 92 and divide by 6 to obtain the **jacket cloth** <term>aobu</term> <note>original: 襖布 (*aobu*); fabric intended for military tunics or linings.</note>. These results match the requirements of the problem.

Now, there are three brothers. The youngest brother said to the eldest: "My age is three-quarters of yours." The second brother's age is five-sixths of the eldest's. The second brother is 8 years older than the youngest. We ask: what are the ages of the three brothers?

->Answer:<-
The eldest brother is **96 years old**.
The second brother is **80 years old**.
The youngest brother is **72 years old**.

# **Huangqi** <note>original: 遠志, Yuǎnzhì; *Polygala tenuifolia*, commonly known as Siberian Milkwort. The name literally translates to "Far-reaching Ambition," reflecting its traditional use in boosting cognitive function and willpower.</note>

**Yuanzhi** is listed as a "superior grade" herb in the *Classic of the Roots and Herbs* <note>original: 本經, Benjing; referring to the *Shennong Ben Cao Jing*, the foundational text of Chinese herbology</note>. In the *Erya* <note>The oldest surviving Chinese dictionary, dating to approximately the 3rd century BCE</note>, it is referred to by the ancient names *Yaorao* <note>original: 葽繞</note> or *Jiyao* <note>original: 棘葽</note>; historical commentary confirms these names refer to the modern **Yuanzhi**. 

The plant resembles **Mahuang** <note>original: 麻黃, Ephedra</note> in its general form, but it bears red flowers and possesses leaves that are notably sharp and yellow. While this description is brief, it captures the essential physical characteristics of the plant perfectly.

The *Shuowen* <note>original: 說文; the *Shuowen Jiezi*, an early 2nd-century dictionary that explains the structure of Chinese characters</note> identifies *Yao* and *Jiyao* as the same plant within its commentary. It is also historically known as the "Yao Grass." Ancient records state that "in the fourth month, the Yao Grass flourishes." The scholar Liu Xiang <note>A noted Han dynasty scholar and editor</note> observed that because this herb has a characteristically bitter taste, it was given the name *Yao* <note>A word often associated with lushness, but here linked by Liu to the plant's potent medicinal properties</note>. 

Consequently, there is some scholarly debate: *Yao* and *Yaorao* might actually be distinct species, though many commentators on the *Classic of Poetry* <note>original: 詩經, Shijing; the oldest existing collection of Chinese poetry</note> simply treat *Yao* as a synonym for **Yuanzhi**.
